newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels advance on copper-rich region.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels advance on copper-rich region.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Wednesday his forces were advancing on several fronts and were closing in on the southeastern town of Moba, gateway to mineral-rich Shaba province.

Kabila, speaking at the opulent lakeside residence formerly used by ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, said his guerrilla army had pursued retreating government forces to within 40 km (25 miles) of Moba.
"We are moving. We are going to deal with Mobutu's forces in Moba within the next few days. I do not see any problem in capturing Moba," Kabila told Reuters.
Asked about government reinforcements being sent to Moba, Kabila laughed: "Mobutu has no army. His (army) generals are mere traders whom we shall defeat across this country.
"There is no other option but to end the suffering of our people caused by Mobutu." added Kabila, surrounded by gun-toting bodyguards.

The advance on Moba follows the seizure by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) of the mining and rail centre of Kalemie, the rebel leaders' hometown. Kalemie is a key port on Lake Tanganyika.
Regional military analysts said Moba's capture would speed a rebel advance on mineral-rich Shaba province, their stated goal.
Kabila said his army, which has had stunning successes since last October, was also advancing on Lubutu, home to Rwanda's ousted 40,000-strong army and more than 100,000 Hutu refugees.

Kabila said his forces were 19 km (12 miles) from Lubutu after capturing a key bridge in a battle that lasted several days. He said they shot down helicopters trying to reinforce pinned-down government troops and their Rwandan Hutu allies.

Kabila said he was ready to open corridors for more than 100,000 Rwandan Hutus trapped in camps around Kisangani and Lubutu and appealed to the U.N. refugee agency to approach him to work out arrangements.
He said 7,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees had crossed over to his forces at the town of Walikale and would be repatriated to their tiny central African nation.

"The resistance has greatly weakened and we should be in Lubutu sooner than soon. We are ready to open up corridors for Rwandans wanting to go back home but those seeking to fight us will be destroyed," he said.
The fall of Lubutu would leave Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, vulnerable and analysts predict it would trigger panic across Africa's third largest country.

Kisangani is now Zaire's key army centre where mercenaries -- said by Kabila to number 300 -- have gathered. Kabila said his forces had killed seven mercenaries and many had been pulled back to Kisangani to rebuild one of the world's most ill-disciplined armies.
Army chief of staff General Mahele Leiko Bokungu, appointed in December with wide-ranging powers, has based his command centre at Kisangani for the last month.

Kabila said his forces, now holding a swathe of land over 1,000 km (600 miles) long, were fighting at Shabunda, home to 35,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, at Kindu, a major airbase, and outside the town of Watsa captured by his troops five days ago.
"We are moving forward. We have built a motivated and dedicated army ready to liberate this country from 31 years of looting, plunder and destruction by Mobutu and his cronies," Kabila said.
